rows.name: Kalymnos
rows.seasonSummary:
April to May and October to November are the classic windows. Conditions are generally comfortable, the island is open for climbers, and both climbing and rest-day life work well.

Summer is hot, though shaded or east-facing options can keep selective climbing possible. Winter can bring unsettled weather and a quieter island, so it is less predictable for a first trip.
rows.transportSummary:
The normal approach is to fly to Kos, then take the ferry to Kalymnos. Flying via Athens to Kalymnos airport is another option when schedules make sense.

Once based around Masouri, Armeos or Myrties, many sectors are walkable. Scooters are popular for reaching farther areas, while Telendos is a short boat trip from Myrties.
rows.accommodationSummary:
Masouri, Armeos and Myrties are the core climbing bases, with hotels, apartments and guesthouses close to food and approaches.

Stay where you can walk to the crags if it is your first visit. The simple village-to-crag rhythm is one of the main reasons Kalymnos works so well.

contentSections.heading: Destination Snapshot
contentSections.body:
Kalymnos is Greek island sport climbing at high density: limestone caves, tufas, pockets, slabs, sea views and walking access from the main villages.

It is one of the simplest places in Europe to build a full climbing holiday around routes, food, swimming and short approaches.

contentSections.heading: Introduction
contentSections.body:
Kalymnos is famous because the climbing is both abundant and easy to use. The main crags sit above Masouri, Armeos and Myrties, many within a manageable walk, with the sea and Telendos behind you all day.

The limestone gives the island its identity: steep orange caves, tufas, blobs, pockets, grey slabs and enough single-pitch sport routes to keep returning climbers busy. There are also bolted multipitch routes, including lines on Telendos.

The logistics are part of the quality. Fly to Kos and take the ferry, or route through Athens to Kalymnos, then settle into a rhythm of morning approaches, long lunches, swimming and evening food in the villages.

contentSections.heading: History
contentSections.body:
Kalymnos grew from a quiet Greek island into a benchmark sport-climbing destination because the rock, access and village logistics lined up almost perfectly.

The area is still developing in places. The existing routes cover only part of the available limestone, and newer sectors have continued to spread the climbing beyond the first classic zones.
warnings: No sourced history and context content found for this pass.

contentSections.heading: Rock and Style
contentSections.body:
The rock is solid limestone, sometimes sharp, with a huge range of shapes. The famous style is steep tufa and stalactite climbing, but the island also has vertical pocket walls, pumpy faces and grey slabs with water pockets.

Most routes are single pitch around 20 to 30 metres, while selected bolted multipitch routes add longer days. The best lines often combine several styles in one pitch: steep start, tufa rest, pocket wall, then a technical finish.

contentSections.heading: Who Is It For
contentSections.body:
Kalymnos suits almost every sport climber. Lower-grade climbers get friendly mileage and clear logistics; intermediate climbers get endless quality; stronger climbers get caves, tufas and hard stamina routes.

It is also a strong group destination because non-climbing time is easy. Beaches, food, scooters and short approaches make the island work even when not everyone climbs the same grade.

contentSections.heading: Grades and Sectors
contentSections.body:
Climb Europe reports more than 4,200 routes from F3a to F9a across 99 sport crags. The range is broad enough that grade alone is not the planning problem; choosing the right sector for sun, wind and style is.

Use a current topo because route counts, extensions and sector details continue to evolve.

contentSections.heading: Best Season
contentSections.body:
April to May and October to November are the classic windows. Conditions are generally comfortable, the island is open for climbers, and both climbing and rest-day life work well.

Summer is hot, though shaded or east-facing options can keep selective climbing possible. Winter can bring unsettled weather and a quieter island, so it is less predictable for a first trip.

contentSections.heading: Gear
contentSections.body:
Bring a sport rack, helmet and a rope suitable for the routes in your topo. Many pitches are 20 to 30 metres, but some are longer, so check before you tie in.

Tape can be useful for sharp rock and tufa days. For multipitch routes, bring proper anchor and descent kit rather than treating them as extended single-pitch climbs.
warnings: No sourced gear and equipment content found for this pass.

contentSections.heading: Getting There
contentSections.body:
The normal approach is to fly to Kos, then take the ferry to Kalymnos. Flying via Athens to Kalymnos airport is another option when schedules make sense.

Once based around Masouri, Armeos or Myrties, many sectors are walkable. Scooters are popular for reaching farther areas, while Telendos is a short boat trip from Myrties.

contentSections.heading: Stay and Eat
contentSections.body:
Masouri, Armeos and Myrties are the core climbing bases, with hotels, apartments and guesthouses close to food and approaches.

Stay where you can walk to the crags if it is your first visit. The simple village-to-crag rhythm is one of the main reasons Kalymnos works so well.

contentSections.heading: Rest Days
contentSections.body:
Rest days are easy: swim, eat, take a boat to Telendos, explore villages or ride north for a slower day.

The island gives you enough recovery options that you do not need to turn every warm or tired day into another redpoint session.

contentSections.heading: Tips and Ethics
contentSections.body:
Plan by sun and wind. West- and south-facing crags can be perfect or brutal depending on the season and time of day.

Do not assume tufas dry quickly after rain. Some steep routes stay climbable, but wet tufas and seepage need patience.
warnings: No sourced practical tips content found for this pass.

contentSections.heading: Safety
contentSections.body:
Wear a helmet, check fixed gear and match rope length to the topo. The island is user-friendly, but it is still limestone sport climbing with variable route lengths.

Be careful with wet tufas. They can take time to dry and are easier to damage or break when damp.

contentSections.heading: Costs and Budget
contentSections.body:
Budget for flights, ferry, accommodation, food, scooter or local transport, guidebook or digital topo access, and rest-day boats if you use them.

Staying in the main climbing villages can cost more than remote bases, but it saves time and keeps the trip simple.

contentSections.body:
When is best? April-May and October-November.

Do I need a car? Not usually around Masouri, Armeos and Myrties. Many crags are walkable, and scooters cover farther sectors.

Is it only hard climbing? No. The route range runs from easy slabs to F9a.

How do I get there? Most climbers fly to Kos and take the ferry.

This is sandstone climbing with culture attached. Some routes are well protected by local standards, others demand comfort with runouts, knots, cracks and the ethics of the Elbsandstein tradition.

contentSections.heading: Destination Snapshot
contentSections.body: Magic Wood is compact Swiss gneiss bouldering in a steep forest valley: over 1,000 problems, hard classics, short links between sectors and conditions that can feel world class when the air is cool and dry.

contentSections.heading: Introduction
contentSections.body:
Magic Wood is small on the map and big in reputation. The boulders sit in forest above the Hinterrhein, giving the area a concentrated feel: you can move between objectives quickly, but the climbing rarely feels easy.

The destination is best known for hard bouldering, yet there are problems across a wider spread. The trick is choosing problems and conditions intelligently rather than assuming the forest will hand out grades.

contentSections.heading: History
contentSections.body:
Magic Wood became famous because a compact valley produced a remarkable density of quality gneiss problems. It is now one of Europe’s standard references for hard forest bouldering.

That popularity makes low-impact behaviour important. Stay on paths, respect camping and parking rules, and avoid turning a small valley into a crowded gym.

contentSections.heading: Rock and Style
contentSections.body:
The rock is Swiss gneiss, with overhangs, crimps, slabs and powerful compression. Many problems are physical, but good footwork still matters.

The forest can hold moisture. When conditions are dry, the rock feels crisp and positive; when humidity rises, hard problems can turn quickly.

contentSections.heading: Who Is It For
contentSections.body:
Magic Wood is best for boulderers who already enjoy outdoor problem solving. Strong climbers will recognize many classics, but intermediates can still build a good trip by choosing carefully.

Beginners should come with realistic expectations, enough pads and partners who can manage landings and sector choice.

contentSections.heading: Grades and Scale
contentSections.body:
Magic Wood has more than 1,000 boulder problems in a compact area of roughly one square kilometre. There is no single clean grade span that captures the area well.

Treat Magic Wood as quality-dense rather than easy-dense. A current topo is essential for finding the right circuits and warm-ups.

contentSections.heading: Season
contentSections.body:
Spring and autumn are the best-supported planning seasons. Summer can work in shade when humidity is acceptable, while winter is usually a poor choice because of seepage and wet conditions.

For any season, dry rock is the real filter.

contentSections.heading: Gear
contentSections.body:
Bring multiple pads, a brush, tape, warm layers and a current topo. Landings vary, and many worthwhile lines climb better with a thoughtful pad stack.

Skin management matters. The gneiss can be sharp enough to end a trip early if you ignore it.

contentSections.heading: Getting There

contentSections.heading: Rest Days
contentSections.body: Rest days can be quiet: river walks, valley views, food runs and skin recovery. The area is compact, so leaving the pads behind is sometimes the smartest decision you make all week.

contentSections.heading: Tips and Ethics
contentSections.body:
Warm up patiently and save skin. Magic Wood has enough famous hard lines to make climbers rush, but the best days come from building into the conditions.

Respect paths, camping rules and other groups. The area’s compactness is a strength only if everyone keeps impact low.

contentSections.heading: Safety

Uneven landings, powerful moves and damp rock are the main concerns. Use enough pads, spot actively and avoid climbing when holds are seeping or wet.

Many problems are close together, so stay aware of pads, people and fall zones around busy classics.

rows.name: Mallorca
rows.seasonSummary:
Spring, autumn and winter are the best windows. The island is quieter, the temperatures are milder, and sport climbing days are much easier to manage than in peak holiday season.

Summer is the weak season for roped climbing. Heat, crowds and strong sun make many venues unpleasant, and deep-water soloing still depends on sea conditions, safe exits and the group staying fresh enough to make good decisions.

Humidity is the common friction tax. Build in flexibility and move between areas rather than forcing a bad crag choice.
rows.transportSummary:
Fly into Palma de Mallorca and rent a car. The island has a useful road network, and a car makes it realistic to switch between mountain crags, coastal sectors and rest-day plans.

Choose the base around the style you want most. The west is practical for many sport areas; the east makes more sense if deep-water soloing is the focus.
rows.accommodationSummary:
Hotels, apartments and villas are the normal island options. A self-catering base works well because climbing days can start early, shift with conditions and finish away from resort restaurant hours.

Stay close to the crags you expect to use most, but do not over-optimize. Mallorca rewards movement, and a slightly longer drive is often worth it for better shade, wind or friction.

contentSections.heading: Destination Snapshot
contentSections.body:
Mallorca is a limestone island trip with two clear personalities: roped sport climbing in the mountains and on coastal cliffs, and deep-water soloing above the Mediterranean.

It works best outside high summer, when the roads, beaches and crags are quieter and the island gives you room to move between sun, shade and sea.

contentSections.heading: Introduction
contentSections.body:
Mallorca is not just a holiday island with a few climbs attached. The western mountains, the coastal walls and the east-coast deep-water solo venues make it a proper climbing destination with enough variety for a full trip.

Sport climbers get limestone walls with tufas, roofs, slabs, cracks and solid everyday mileage. Deep-water soloing gives the island its sharper edge: sea cliffs, clear water, committing movement and days where conditions matter as much as grade.

The best plan is to choose a base, rent a car, and keep the week flexible. Mallorca is small enough to cross without losing the day, but varied enough that orientation, wind and humidity can make one crag feel perfect while another feels wrong.

contentSections.heading: History
contentSections.body:
Mallorca has a long modern guidebook history. Winter sport climbing on the island came to wider attention in the late 1980s, and the first Rockfax guide appeared in 1995 with 12 sport crags.

The island scene is now bigger and more mature. Roped sport climbing and deep-water soloing have enough depth to stand as separate styles, which is exactly how many visiting climbers plan the trip.

contentSections.heading: Rock and Style
contentSections.body:
Expect Mediterranean limestone with a broad spread of movement. Some walls are steep and athletic, with tufas, roofs and big holds. Others are more technical, with slabs, cracks and vertical faces where footwork matters.

The sport climbing is concentrated around the western side of the island and the mountain approaches near Palma and Soller, with additional east-coast sport venues. Deep-water soloing is a different day entirely: coastal cliffs, sea-state decisions, exits and a much more serious consequence model.

Humidity can take the snap out of the rock. On damp days, choose orientation carefully and do not expect perfect friction just because the sky is blue.

contentSections.heading: Who Is It For
contentSections.body:
Mallorca suits climbers who like variety more than single-crag routine. A mixed group can combine sport days, easier mileage, harder limestone objectives and rest days without changing destination.

Sport climbing is the simpler choice for most visitors. Deep-water soloing is for confident climbers who understand the sea, the fall zone and the need to walk away when conditions are wrong.

Rest days are easy here. Swim, walk the coast, visit mountain villages, eat properly and let the island do some of the recovery work.

If humidity or heat makes the climbing poor, use the day rather than fighting it. Mallorca has enough non-climbing value that a rest day does not feel wasted.

contentSections.heading: Tips and Ethics
contentSections.body:
Plan by orientation. Sun, humidity and wind are often more important than the shortest drive from the apartment.

For deep-water soloing, do not copy someone else into the water. Check depth, swell, exits and your own margin. If in doubt, climb sport routes or take the rest day.

contentSections.heading: Safety
contentSections.body:
Limestone, sea cliffs and holiday-mode decision making are the main hazards. Wear a helmet for roped climbing, check lower-offs, and use recent topos for route length and access.

Deep-water soloing is not controlled falling into a swimming pool. Sea state, hidden rocks, changing water levels, awkward exits and fatigue all matter.

contentSections.heading: Costs and Budget
contentSections.body:
Budget for flights to Palma, car hire, accommodation, fuel and topo access. Island prices rise in peak holiday periods, another reason climbing trips usually feel better outside summer.

contentSections.heading: Hero
contentSections.body: A Carinthian alpine valley for granite and gneiss climbing, best known for bouldering but strong for sport routes and multi-pitches too.

contentSections.heading: Introduction
contentSections.body:
Maltatal sits in Austria's southern Alps, following the Malta river through a high valley of blocks, sport crags and longer routes. It is best known as a bouldering area, but the same valley gives enough roped climbing to make it useful for mixed teams.

The character is crisp and technical: crimps, slabs, rounded holds, short approaches and a mountain setting where conditions can be chosen by elevation. It is a good destination when you want quiet rock days rather than a resort-style climbing town.

contentSections.heading: History and context
contentSections.body: Maltatal's bouldering reputation is tied to hard lines and local development. Gerhard Schaar is a central local developer and guidebook figure, while Klem Loskot's ascent of Bugeleisen stand helped push the area onto the international bouldering map.
warnings: No sourced history and context content found for this pass.

contentSections.heading: Rock and climbing character
contentSections.body:
The rock is described locally as solid gneiss, while the broader climbing profile is granite-family alpine valley climbing. In practice the climbing is technical: crimps, slabs, rounded slopers, steep problems and some crack features.

For roped climbing, the valley has single-pitch sport routes and multi-pitches. For bouldering, the main style rewards finger strength, precise footwork and comfort on small holds.

contentSections.heading: Who it suits
contentSections.body:
Maltatal works for boulderers first, but it should not be boxed in as bouldering-only. Sport climbers in lower and middle grades have useful options, and multi-pitch climbers can add longer alpine-feeling days.

It is a particularly good fit for climbers who like technical movement and do not need nightlife or dense town logistics after climbing.

contentSections.heading: Grades and difficulty
contentSections.body: The supported roped-climbing picture is about 25 sport crags, around 350 single-pitch sport routes and 70 multi-pitch routes, with many sport routes between 5a and 7c. The bouldering count used here is more than 300 problems.

For bouldering, bring pads, shoes, chalk and enough spotters for uneven landings. For sport climbing, pack a normal rack and an 80 m rope for the longest single pitches.

Multi-pitch days need standard longer-route kit, with approaches ranging from short walks to more committed mountain starts.

contentSections.heading: Destination Snapshot
contentSections.body: Margalef is steep Catalan sport climbing on pocketed conglomerate: short approaches, powerful sequences, endurance routes and enough lines from F4 to F9b+ to keep a team busy for weeks.

contentSections.heading: Introduction
contentSections.body:
Margalef sits in the Montsant region and has become one of Spain’s clearest answers to the question: where do we go for pocketed sport climbing with real depth?

The style is distinctive. You pull on cobbles, pockets and edges, often on walls that are steeper than they first look. The village is small, the sectors are numerous, and a car-based week lets you chase shade, sun and grade bands without wasting much energy.

contentSections.heading: History
contentSections.body:
Margalef’s reputation comes from modern sport-climbing development and the sheer productivity of the rock. It is a destination where hard climbing is visible, but the area is not only for elite grades.

The best trip rhythm is local and simple: climb, rest, eat, check skin and fingers, then pick the next sector by conditions.

contentSections.heading: Rock and Style
contentSections.body:
The rock is conglomerate, with pockets as the headline. Some routes are finger-intensive and bouldery; others build into long resistance pitches where reading the rests matters as much as pulling hard.

Expect overhangs, positive pockets, small edges and the occasional sequence that feels strange until you trust the feet. Skin and finger care are part of the destination.

contentSections.heading: Who Is It For
contentSections.body:
Margalef works for sport climbers who like steep movement and projecting, especially from the 6s upward. Strong intermediates and advanced climbers get the most obvious value from the density.

There are easier routes in the range, but this is not the softest first outdoor sport venue. Climbers should be comfortable reading bolts, resting well and managing pockets carefully.

contentSections.heading: Grades and Scale
contentSections.body:
Margalef has more than 1,600 sport routes from F4 to F9b+. That is enough range for mixed groups, but the character still leans toward pocketed sport climbing rather than gentle mileage.

Use a current topo to choose sectors by grade density, aspect and approach.

contentSections.heading: Season
contentSections.body:
Spring and autumn are the main planning seasons. Shaded summer climbing can be possible, but heat management becomes part of the day.

Start early, pick aspect carefully and keep rest days available if the forecast turns too hot for pockets.

contentSections.heading: Gear
contentSections.body:
Bring a sport rack with enough quickdraws for the chosen sector, a rope appropriate to current topo lengths, helmet, belay glasses if you use them, and tape for pocket-worn fingers.

For projecting, pack kneepads only if the topo and route style justify them. Do not assume every sector climbs the same.

contentSections.heading: Getting There
contentSections.body:
Flying to Barcelona and renting a car is the practical plan. Margalef is rural, and sector choice is much easier with a vehicle.

Build drives, parking and food runs into the day rather than treating the village as a full-service resort.

contentSections.heading: Stay and Eat
contentSections.body:
Campsites, apartments and guesthouse-style bases are the main lodging categories to plan around. Confirm named options before booking.

For a climbing week, prioritize cooking access, drying space and easy car logistics over hotel polish.

contentSections.heading: Rest Days
contentSections.body: Rest days can stay local in the Montsant landscape: walking, village time, slow meals and finger recovery. Siurana and other Catalan climbing areas are close enough to tempt a change of scene, but skin often needs a real break.

contentSections.heading: Tips and Ethics
contentSections.body:
Choose sectors by finger condition as much as by grade. Pocketed conglomerate can feel friendly for one session and harsh by day three.

Respect parking, paths and quiet village life. Margalef works because climbing and the small local base still fit together.

contentSections.heading: Safety
contentSections.body:
Pocket injuries are the obvious climbing-specific risk. Warm up properly, avoid reckless mono or two-finger loading, and step back if fingers feel tweaky.

Wear a helmet where rockfall or crowded belays make it sensible, and check route length before lowering.

contentSections.heading: Introduction
contentSections.body:
Rodellar sits in the Sierra de Guara and has a very clear identity. This is sport climbing built around steep limestone, tufas and resistance, with many of the best days spent fighting pump rather than searching for holds.

The village and canyon create a compact destination rhythm. Walk in, choose shade, climb long pitches, recover slowly, and accept that the style rewards fitness, kneebars and patience.

contentSections.heading: History
contentSections.body:
Rodellar’s modern reputation comes from the rise of steep limestone sport climbing. The canyon walls turned into a reference point for endurance routes, tufas and hard redpointing.

It remains more than a hard-climber venue, but its character is unmistakable: this is a place to learn how to rest, sequence and climb efficiently on steep stone.

contentSections.heading: Rock and Style
contentSections.body:
The rock is limestone with tufas, caves, pockets and sustained overhangs. Many routes are long enough that clipping strategy and shake-outs matter.

Expect three-dimensional climbing: knees, heels, drop-knees, compression and body positions that save forearms when the wall keeps leaning.

contentSections.heading: Who Is It For
contentSections.body:
Rodellar is best for sport climbers who enjoy endurance and steep terrain. The strongest density sits from 7a to 8b, with classics starting from grade 5 upward.

Beginners can find options, but the destination makes most sense for climbers who already lead outside and want to improve on steep limestone.

contentSections.heading: Destination Snapshot
contentSections.body:
Terradets is Catalan limestone in a gorge setting north of Lleida, famous for hard sport climbing at Paret de les Bruixes and long multipitch terrain nearby.

It is a winter and shoulder-season venue for climbers who like steep stamina, tufas, pockets and technical limestone logistics.

contentSections.heading: Introduction
contentSections.body:
Terradets sits in the southern Pyrenean runoffs, in the wider Lleida climbing belt. The name often points first to Paret de les Bruixes, a steep sport sector known for hard seventh- and lower eighth-grade routes, but the area has more than one personality.

Paret de les Bagasses brings the bigger wall: a limestone face up to around 500 metres, with multipitch history and a very different day out. Around Cellers, the logistics are compact enough that accommodation, station access and crag movement can line up well.

The climbing is conditions-sensitive. Shade, fog from the reservoir, polished rock and winter friction all matter. Terradets rewards climbers who are willing to wait for the right hour rather than rushing onto the wall.

contentSections.heading: History
contentSections.body:
Terradets belongs to the classic Lleida sport-climbing landscape, alongside names such as Camarasa and Sant Llorenc de Montgai. Its modern reputation is tied strongly to Les Bruixes and the wave of hard sport development there.

The older big-wall identity has not disappeared. Paret de les Bagasses keeps Terradets connected to long-route climbing as well as redpoint sport.

Paret de les Bagasses gives a different scale, with long routes on a 500-metre wall. Treat those days with multipitch seriousness, not sport-sector habits.

contentSections.heading: Who Is It For

Terradets suits strong sport climbers first, especially those comfortable in the hard seventh and lower eighth grades. That is where Les Bruixes has its clearest reputation.

It can also work for climbers seeking easier routes or multipitch objectives, but they should plan carefully rather than assuming the famous sector will fit everyone.

Late autumn and winter are strong for Les Bruixes, where shade and polished rock make friction important. Spring and autumn can work well across the wider area.

rows.name: Zillertal
rows.seasonSummary:
Spring, summer and autumn are the supported seasons. Altitude, aspect and weather decide which style is best on a given day.

Summer can be productive in mountain conditions, while spring and autumn may offer better friction when dry.
rows.transportSummary:
A car is recommended. Innsbruck, Munich and Salzburg are useful airport references, but exact driving times and road conditions should be checked for the chosen base.

Within the valley, independent transport gives the best chance of chasing weather and aspect.
rows.accommodationSummary:
Zillertal has enough styles that the best base depends on the trip focus. Valley guesthouses and campsites work well for mixed cragging and bouldering; huts or higher bases make more sense when longer mountain objectives are the plan.

Food, drying space and flexibility matter more than being closest to one sector.

contentSections.heading: Destination Snapshot
contentSections.body: Zillertal is a Tyrolean valley climbing area with sport routes, multi-pitches and bouldering on granite: a mountain base where one forecast can send you to slabs, cracks, crags or blocks.

contentSections.heading: Introduction
contentSections.body:
Zillertal is broad enough to behave like a climbing region rather than one crag. The area has 500 single- and multi-pitch routes plus 1,000 boulders, giving mixed groups room to adapt.

The valley setting is the point. You can build a trip around sport climbing, bouldering or longer routes, then adjust by weather, skin, partners and energy.

contentSections.heading: History
contentSections.body:
Zillertal’s climbing identity comes from its alpine valley geography and granite variety. It is not defined by one wall or one grade band, but by the ability to switch styles within the same trip.

That makes planning more important. A good week uses the whole valley intelligently instead of forcing the same sector every day.

contentSections.heading: Rock and Style
contentSections.body:
The main rock type is granite, with cracks and slabs as key features. Expect technical footwork, friction climbing and occasional crack systems rather than limestone pocket pulling.

Because the area spans roped and bouldering venues, rock character changes by sector. A current routebook is important.

contentSections.heading: Who Is It For
contentSections.body:
Zillertal suits climbers who want options. Sport climbers, boulderers and multi-pitch teams can all find objectives if they plan by conditions and ability.

It is especially good for groups that do not all want the same style every day.

contentSections.heading: Grades and Scale
contentSections.body:
Zillertal has 500 single- and multi-pitch routes plus 1,000 boulders. There is no clean single grade range for the whole valley, so grades should be handled through current topo choice rather than broad claims.

Use the count to understand scale, not to choose objectives.

contentSections.heading: Season
contentSections.body:
Spring, summer and autumn are the supported seasons. Altitude, aspect and weather decide which style is best on a given day.

Summer can be productive in mountain conditions, while spring and autumn may offer better friction when dry.

contentSections.heading: Gear
contentSections.body:
Pack for the style you intend to climb: sport rack, bouldering pads or multi-pitch kit as needed. Granite-specific extras such as tape, brushes, helmets and warmer layers are sensible.

Do not rely on one generic gear list for the whole valley.

contentSections.heading: Getting There
contentSections.body:
A car is recommended. Innsbruck, Munich and Salzburg are useful airport references, but exact driving times and road conditions should be checked for the chosen base.

Within the valley, independent transport gives the best chance of chasing weather and aspect.

contentSections.heading: Stay and Eat
contentSections.body:
Zillertal has enough styles that the best base depends on the trip focus. Valley guesthouses and campsites work well for mixed cragging and bouldering; huts or higher bases make more sense when longer mountain objectives are the plan.

Food, drying space and flexibility matter more than being closest to one sector.

contentSections.heading: Rest Days
contentSections.body: Rest days can stay active with valley walks, mountain views and Tyrolean village time. Because the destination is varied, a rest day can also mean changing style lightly, but skin and shoulders may prefer a genuine break.

contentSections.heading: Tips and Ethics
contentSections.body:
Use Zillertal’s variety. If boulders are damp, consider roped climbing; if the sun is too strong, change aspect or altitude.

Check local parking and access before driving into side valleys.

contentSections.heading: Safety
contentSections.body:
Mountain weather, uneven boulder landings, granite friction changes and multi-pitch commitment are the main concerns. Match the day to the forecast and the team.

For roped climbing, confirm route length and descent. For bouldering, pad uneven landings carefully.

How big is the climbing area? 500 roped routes plus 1,000 boulders.

When should I go? Spring, summer and autumn are the supported seasons.

rows.title: Novice course
rows.shortDescription: Beginner climbers get ready to embrace the face. Rockbusters’ novice courses are a great way to catch the climbing bug. Whether you’re a complete rookie or just looking to make the step from indoor to outdoor climbing, this course will tick all your boxes. Tackle the basics head on, master technique and learn to climb safely. Get your head around all the gear and equipment you’ll need to stay safe and crank your way up the face. At Rockbusters it’s not just about technique, but immersing yourself in the complete climbing experience, with guides who live and breath to climb. So not only will you have an awesome time learning but you’ll enjoy a fun party atmosphere in the camp. Our top coaches will be with you every step of the way helping you to master the following:

catalogueCard.title: Novice Climbing Course
catalogueCard.description: Move from indoor climbing to real rock with basics, belaying, movement, safety skills, and a full Rockbusters camp week.

children.text: What equipment you need and how to choose it so you have the best climbing experience while staying safe
Technical climbing skills like how to belay, set up top-rope and lead climb (depending on your level)
Climbing calls and communication so that you can get your message across to climbing buddies
Movement skills to help you climb more efficiently
Basic understanding of outdoor risks so you can make it home safely every day
Cleaning the anchors so you can retrieve all your gear

At the end of the course, our aim is to have transformed you into a competent independent climber tackling routes you would not have believed yourself capable of. You’ll be moving like a mountain goat, be more honed, and have a firm grasp of belay for top rope and leading. Plus you’ll know all the relevant communication and climbing terminology.

This course is a great way into climbing culture. It’s intense for sure, but this means you’ll develop your skills quickly and progress way faster than you thought possible. Join the Rockbusters Novice Camp and you’ll quickly reach new heights and be ready to take on epic routes you could only dream of.

There are big roofs, overhangs and high balls aplenty, as well as slabs of all grades. And if you deck out, it’s never a big drop.

rows.title: Trad and Multipitch
rows.shortDescription: Who wants to get really high? No, not like that you naughty people. We’re talking about taking the huge step from single pitch fixed anchor climbing to multi-pitch and trad climbing (traditional climbing is placing your own protection and fixing your own anchors). If you don’t try, you’ll never know how high or far you can go. If you’ve mastered the climbing basics and are keen to really push yourself then let the Rockbusters crew get you high.

catalogueCard.title: Trad & Multipitch Climbing
catalogueCard.description: Move from single-pitch climbing into trad and multi-pitch routes with technical coaching for bigger, higher objectives.

children.text: The trad and multipitch course are a test of nerves as you start putting some real distance between yourself and the ground. You’ll focus on multipitch rope skills and techniques that will keep you safe at pant-filling heights. You’ll get a good grounding (if you’ll pardon the pun) in all the equipment and how to choose the right gear for the climb. You’ll also learn how to look after your gear properly, increasing it’s life and possibly saving yours.
Specific skills you’ll learn include:
Building safe belays to get a better understanding of rope technique
Abseils and retreats for getting yourself back down to terra firma
Climbing calls and communication so you can get your message across to other climbers
Self-rescue skills - worth knowing if you want to make it home safely
Learn how to use a climbing guide book so you can climb in new areas and safely plan your routes
You’ll develop a good understanding of climbing risks and when to retreat or not climb at all

rows.title: Czech Sandstone
rows.shortDescription: If you’re familiar with British gritstone then Czech sandstone will be surprisingly similar. If you’ve got no idea what we’re talking about then all you need to know is that the Czech sandstone of the Elbe Mountains is one of the best rock types for climbing.

catalogueCard.title: Czech Sandstone
catalogueCard.description: Experience Elbe sandstone climbing, unique ethics, and technical movement on one of Europe's most distinctive rock types.

children.text: This is your chance to experience some of the most unique and exciting Czech climbing, accompanied by some of the finest guides you could ever wish to meet (even if we do say so ourselves). It’s perfect for climbers who’ve got a fair bit of experience under their belt, but open to anyone who can belay safely and tie on without assistance.

For Indoor climbers it is the ideal first step into outdoor climbing - you’ll get a kick out of testing your skills in the open. The Elbe Mountains are considered by many as one of the best sandstone climbing destinations on the planet.
On this trip you’ll add to your arsenal of climbing skills:
Top-roping and lead climbing - someone has to tackle the face first
Equipment use, storage and maintenance to help it last well and keep you safe
How to use a guide book so you can explore new areas and pick your own routes
Movement skills so you can traverse the face and build technique and strength
Understanding of outdoor risks so you don’t make any rookie mistakes

Throughout your stay you’ll be guided by a local climber and route developer who’ll use their local knowledge to take you deep into the Elbe sandstone. These ancient rocks straddle the border between German Saxony and Czech Bohemia and are, not surprisingly, a national park. The River Elbe has carved a narrow gorge through the soft sandstone, creating some stunning cracks and crevices that will get serious climbers pretty aroused.

All of this climbing is accompanied by the legendary Rockbusters good time experience. We know how to climb and we know how to party, and we want to do both with you. Come and be part of the crew in this top Czech mountain destination.
For those who are just starting out, check out our other courses for beginners and intermediate climbers and use this as a goal to work towards. You won’t regret it.

rows.title: Sport Climbing Camp
rows.shortDescription: For the Rockbusters team climbing is not just a sport, it’s what we eat, drink, breathe and sleep - it’s what we live for. Our Sport Climbing Camp gives you the opportunity to get a taste of what we mean and become part of our climbing crew. Come and join us for a week or two in one of the best European crags. You’ll get to spend all day on the face, taking on as many climbs as your fingers can handle. Then, it’s all back to camp to kick back and relax as hard as you want to - living the climbing life we love.

catalogueCard.title: Sport Climbing Camp
catalogueCard.description: A week or two of sport climbing, performance coaching, and camp life at some of Europe's best crags.

children.text: During the Sport Climbing Camp we’ll provide one-on-one coaching, video and photo analysis to help improve your performance. This is really useful for climbers who already have some outdoor experience and who want to hone their technique and to get deeper into the climbing culture.
During your stay you’ll get:
On-going performance coaching so that you’re always building on your technique
Time on slab and vertical ground to improve footwork for better climbing
Work on balance so that you climb in a more efficient way (leading F5 or more)
Overhang work to build strength and confidence so you can take on tougher climbing challenges
Tuition for difficult routes of F6 or more for more experienced climbers looking to move up the grades
Red point and on-sight attempts so you can tackle new climbs more easily

The focus of our Sport Climbing Camp is on quality climbing, so it’s aimed at climbers with some experience. Beginners might be more suited to our Novice course, which is equally intense but in a different way. We will push you to achieve more during your stay,arming you with all the necessary techniques and safety measures before you try anything new.

You’ll be shown how to use a guidebook so you can read the topo and figure out new climbing areas for yourself. We’ll develop your calls and communication so you can stay in touch with other climbers on the face, and communicate with those at the base. You’ll learn about cleaning anchors and safe belaying for top rope and leading. Basically, everything we know we’ll try and pass on to you. And that’s a heck of a lot.
Our Sport Climbing Camp gives you a little glimpse of what it’s like to lead the climbing life. This is who we are and what we do, and we’d love the chance to show just why we do it every day. .

rows.title: Europe  Climbing Trip
rows.shortDescription: The European Climbing Road Trip is Rockbusters favourite time of the year. How could it not be? Driving across pretty much the whole of Europe throughout the summer, stopping at all the climbing crags we think are worth it. It’s an awesome experience and our guests seem to think so too, which is why we do it year after year. Our road trip is a unique climbing experience that you can dip in or out of as you wish. You can join us the whole way or come for one or two of your favourite sections. The atmosphere on the tour is legendary, with everyone becoming part of a big family. We have to admit, it’s hard to say goodbye, but then people often come back the following year so it’s not so bad.

catalogueCard.title: European Climbing Road Trip
catalogueCard.description: Join the Rockbusters road trip across Europe's standout crags. Drop in for one section or stay for the full tour.

children.text: We’ll introduce you to loads of different places, including top climbing spots like the German Frankenjura, Spanish Margalef and French Ceuse. We guarantee you fantastic climbing, top tuition and guidance, as well as the most fun you can have on a climbing tour.

Of course, we recommend that you join our crew for the whole tour but we know that some of you have proper jobs and other commitments. That’s fine just choose the destinations or dates that work for you and come along for as long as you want - we’ll even pick you up from a nearby airport.
Our performance coaching is ongoing throughout the tour so here’s what you’ll learn (amongst many other life lessons):
What equipment you need and how to choose it properly to have a great climbing experience whilst staying safe
How to belay, set up top-rope and lead climbing to develop more technical climbing skills
Using a guide book, climbing calls and communication so that you can tackle new climbing areas in the future
Movement skills for more efficient climbing
Understanding of outdoor risks so you can make it home safely every day
Cleaning the anchors so you can retrieve all your gear safel
y

As well as all this, we’ll focus on slab/vertical ground and footwork. We’ll teach you how to use your balance and how to place your feet to efficiently move on the rock (leading comfortably F5 or more). You’ll develop skills to help you handle steep faces, save energy and climb more confidently and efficiently (leading comfortably F6c or more), with some work on overhangs too.

For climbers who are confident enough with their balance, foot work and who have already acquired the basics of climbing technique, we will move on to on-sight/red point. This means we can focus on more challenging routes (leading F6c and above).

The focus for the tour is epic climbing, meaning you can take on loads of routes each day and spend plenty of time on the face. And rest assured that our instructors will make sure everyone has fully mastered new techniques before trying them out for real.

We think you’ll agree that our itinerary is pretty spectacular. Here’s where the tour stops:
Labské údolí - Czech republic

The Elbe Mountains are without doubt one of the best sandstone areas in Europe, forming the border between the Czech Republic and Germany. The River Elbe carves its way through the soft sandstone creating steep sided gorges and crags that are begging to be climbed. It’s very challenging for technical sport climbing and generally considered suitable for climbers capable of leading 6a’s and harder. If you’ve got a bit of experience under your belt then this is a great place to improve your technique and mental control – becoming a Zen climbing master.
Fly via Prague, arrive Saturday and depart Saturday allowing 6 days climbing Sunday to Friday.
Frankenjura - Germany

One of the biggest and best climbing spots in Germany and probably Europe too. Located between Nuremberg, Bamberg and Bayreuth there are about 1,000 crags to explore in the area, which is enough to keep anyone busy. Most routes are short, powerful single pitch sport climbs on limestone with plenty of finger pockets. With around 10,000 routes, this is perfect for climbers of all levels. It’s also family-friendly and a top spot to start leading or to do your first outdoor climbs all backdropped by the beautiful forests of Bavaria. There’s accommodation to suit most needs and budgets in campsites or guesthouses.
Fly via Nürnberg, Germany: arrive Saturday and depart Saturday allowing 6 days climbing Sunday to Friday.
Zillertal - Austria

The undisputed best granite climbing spot in the Tirol, bar none. There are around 700 routes to climb, seven via ferratas, climbing gardens and lots of pitch tours. With so many options you can climb here until your fingers bleed (hopefully not of course!). We usually say that some outdoor climbing experience and leading may be relevant but not essential, and there are plenty of routes for all abilities. We love this stop on the tour and think you will too. Accommodation is in a local campsite.
Fly to München, Germany. Fly from Milano, Italy: arrive Saturday and depart Saturday allowing 6 days climbing Monday to Friday.
Finale Ligure - Italy

With the Czech Republic, Germany and Austria done, Italy is the next logical stop. And what a stop it is. The climbing at Finale Ligure is stunning. With around 2,700 routes to choose on white limestone rocks in an area of about 10 square kilometres, this is one of the best climbing areas in Italy. The deep green landscape can be harsh and wild, and it’s not your usual climbing area, but then again, this is not your usual climbing tour either. It’s the perfect place for experienced climbers to go hard and beginners to bag their first crags. The free camping area is a nice bonus too.
Fly to Milano, Italy. Fly from Torino, Italy: arrive Saturday and depart Saturday allowing 6 days climbing Sunday to Friday.
Ceüse – France

The best sports climbing crag in France and maybe even the world, this is a no brainer stop off point for our tour. Blessed with beautifully pocketed limestone, amazing lines and a truly stunning location, this is a climbing nivannah that is not to be missed. Most routes are single pitch and the climbing is really varied, ranging from overhangs to steep technical walls. The routes are renowned for being tough and requiring plenty of stamina so they are mostly suitable for climbers with some outdoor climbing experience and good fitness. Leading experience is also relevant but not essential. Accommodation in Ceüse is in a campsite.
Fly into Torino, Italy. Fly back from Montpellier, France:  arrive Saturday and depart Saturday allowing 6 days climbing Sunday to Friday.
19/9/2015  26/9/2015  Gorge du Tarn - France

Situated in the south-west of France in the Pyrenees, this is a well-known spot for bouldering and sports climbing. The rock here is good and well-bolted with the Gorge du Tarn offering excellent steep overhangs that will test the stamina of even experienced climbers. There’s a good spread of grades so something for all ability levels to get stuck into. Some routes are up to 150m long. Again, it’s suitable for sport climbers with at least some outdoor climbing experience and being able to lead climb is relevant but not essential. Accommodation is also in a campsite.
Fly via Montpelliere, France: arrive Saturday and depart Saturday allowing 6 days climbing Sunday to Friday.
Margalef – Spain

Considered a climbing paradise by some, Margalef in Spain is located near to Montsant and Siurana. With more than 500 routes of all types, quality and grades. There’s big overhangs, small pockets, tufas, boulder routes and plenty more to try out. It’s all found in nearly 50 crags spread over two valleys, with climbs of all grades including slabs, overhangs and vertical walls. It’s an incredibly beautiful place too. It’s suitable for sport climbers with at least some outdoor climbing experience. Leading is helpful but not essential. Accommodation is in a local campsite.
Fly via Barcelona/Llerida, Spain: arrive Saturday and depart Saturday allowing 6 days climbing Sunday to Friday.
Rodellar - Spain

The last stop on the tour is appropriately one of the world's best climbing areas. We’ll take on athletic, long stamina climbs in huge caves and there’s another chance to improve your tufa technique. This is mostly advanced sport climbing and suitable for climbers with outdoor climbing experience although there are plenty of easy routes to enjoy if you are less experienced. But by this time on the tour, you should be able to take on the challenge. Leading experience is not essential, but very welcome. Accommodation is in an excellent refuge within walking distance of the crags.
Fly via Barcelona, Spain: arrive Saturday and depart Saturday allowing 6 days climbing Sunday to Friday.

So, as you can see, this is a pretty comprehensive European tour stopping at many of Europe’s legendary climbing spots. Join the crew from the start and travel the whole way or pick your favorite destination and we’ll meet you there. However you do it, being part of our European tour you’ll become part of the Rockbusters family, live the life and become a better climber. What’s not to like?

This is a climbing trip and our number one goal is to maximize your time spent on the rock.

We strongly suggest bringing a down jacket, a hat, a rain jacket, a pair of comfortable approach shoes, a headlamp, a sleeping bag, and a backpack big enough for carrying lunch and gear to the crag.

There is a basic shared accommodation organized by Rockbusters. Our main goal is to integrate you into the local climbing communities and for these purposes, we use local climbing hostels, cottages, campsites, or places run by local climbers. Feel free to reach out to adjust these settings to your personal satisfaction.

In Labske Udoli, Frankenjura, Finale Ligure, Zillertal, Margalef, and Rodellar we stay in hostels or campsites bungalows with bunk beds. In Gorges du Tarn we use permanent caravans which belong to the campsite and in Ceuse we stay in campsites with hot showers, wi-fi, a restaurant, ..., we provide tents so you will need to bring a sleeping bag and foam pad.

Upon arrival, we will take you to the store to shop for breakfast and lunch food for the week. Refrigerators are provided by the campsite, and we will return to the store once more during the week to replenish supplies.
There are options to cook individually, in groups or eat outside.

rows.title: Rockbusters coaching - On Sight / Red Point
rows.shortDescription: Are you looking to maximize and develop your climbing skills? Of course you are, who isn’t and that’s why you’re on our site, right? Well, you’re in luck because that’s exactly what our Coaching Programme offers. We’ll help you to improve grade and through better technique no matter what your starting level.

catalogueCard.title: On-Sight & Redpoint Coaching
catalogueCard.description: Build better tactics for on-sight and redpoint attempts, from reading routes to executing when it matters.

children.text: We focus on balance and movement, which helps both your physical and mental development. Whether you’re a complete rookie or an experienced cranker, you’ll notice a rapid improvement once we’ve analysed and boosted your technique.

Increase your confidence and performance through plenty of practice and consolidation at each level. This allows you to head home having gained the most possible from your trip. Climb higher, faster, stronger and better. That’s what we’re all looking for on the face and in life.
Here’s a little look at what to expect when you join Rockbusters Coaching Programme.
Slab/vertical ground
Focusing on footwork, you will learn how to work with your balance, finding the most efficient and effective way to move on the rock (leading comfortably F5 or more).
Overhangs

You will experience a wide range of techniques and skills in practice, which will increase your confidence and performance while climbing overhangs. You’ll develop skills to help you handle climbing steep rocks, save energy and climb more confidently and efficiently (leading comfortably F6c or more).
Onsight / red point

This part of the course is well-suited to climbers who are confident enough with their balance, foot work and overhang technics, and who want to focus on more challenging routes (leading F6c and above).

As well as building confidence, strength and taking on some tough climbs, this is a Rockbusters course so you can also expect a hefty dollop of fun. We love what we do and that really comes across in all our tours and programmes. We like to party almost as much as we like to climb, so get ready to have a blast on and off the face.
Maximum 4 clients per instructor!

rows.title: Christmas Climbing Camp
rows.shortDescription: Christmas – it’s a time for over-indulgence, rubbish presents, annoying family members and board games (or should that be bored games?). Or it could be your chance to crank some of Europe’s best crags. It’s your call but we know where we’ll be and we strongly recommend you come and join us.

catalogueCard.title: Christmas Climbing Camp
catalogueCard.description: Swap the usual Christmas routine for sunny crags, Rockbusters camp life, and a festive climbing crew.

children.text: The Rockbusters Christmas Climbing Camp is your chance to get away from all the drudgery of the Christmas holidays and get out on the face. The destination for our Christmas camps is pretty special too. Sella is the most extensive climbing area in the Costa Blanca with hundreds of sport routes and slabs to explore. In the summer it can get a little busy here but at this time of year you’ll find some really peaceful and empty crags to attack.

Climb as much as you want and we’ll provide you with our expert one-on-one coaching, video and photo analysis. If you’ve already got a bit of climbing experience (or none at all but are bursting with enthusiasm!) and are looking to take it to the next level then this is the perfect time to do it.
Our Christmas camp focuses on:
Slab/vertical ground to improve footwork and climbing efficiency
Balance and foot placement to develop better technique for more confident climbing (leading comfortably F5 or more)
Overhangs and steep sections to develop strength and confidence (leading comfortably F6c or more)
On-sight/red point aimed at climbers who are confident enough with their balance, footwork and have already acquired the basics of climbing technique
Beginners will be taught the basics and fast tracked into the climbing community
On the Christmas Climbing Camp we focus on having fun and racking up as much face time as possible. Whatever your level we will set you challenging routes to help you improve as a climber.

This is a Rockbusters course so you know it’s not all going to be about the climbing. We live and breathe the sport but we also know how to have a good time. Plus, this is Christmas so it’s an extra special reason to party. Rockbusters is more like a family than a tour company so you’ll feel right at home at this special time of year. And we promise not to give you any rubbish presents.

On the end for this week you will be fed up by climbing but hungry for more in the same time. Of course you can expect cool progress and confidence boost.
This is a climbing trip and our number one goal is to maximize your time spent on the rock.
Worries free climbing vacation. Book your flights and leave rest to us. We sort out all logistics for you.

We provide all the gear, but you will need to bring your own reasonably tight climbing shoes and harness. We have belay devices, slings, and helmets, but you might prefer to bring your own. We strongly suggest bringing a down jacket, a hat, a rain jacket, a pair of comfortable approach shoes, head lamp, sleeping bag, and a backpack big enough for carrying lunch and gear to the crag.

We gonna be accommodated in mountain cottage (7€ voluntary doination a night). Basic, sleeping on the mattresses under the roof but no tens are needed. There is stove to use for cooking, fire place to heat up, hot shower, ... and it is 50m from closest crag. More info and pics when booking/inquiring.

rows.title: Easter Climbing in SELLA
rows.shortDescription: At Easter we all get some time off but most people spend it doing little else than stuffing their faces with chocolate. But this could be the perfect opportunity to crank some of Europe’s best crags. It definitely beats getting indigestion.

catalogueCard.title: Easter Climbing in Sella
catalogueCard.description: Spend Easter climbing Sella's Costa Blanca limestone instead of staying home, with Rockbusters coaching and crag time.

children.text: The Rockbusters Easter Climbing Camp is your chance to get out on the face during your holidays. Our destination is Sella, the most extensive climbing area in the Costa Blanca. There are hundreds of sport routes and slabs to crank. And at this time of year you’ll find some really peaceful and empty crags to climb.

Climb as much as you want and we’ll provide you with our expert one-on-one video and photo analysis. If you’ve already got a bit of climbing experience and are looking to take it to the next level then this is the perfect time to do it.

Slab/vertical ground to improve footwork and climbing efficiency

On-sight/red point aimed at climbers who are confident enough with their balance, footwork and have already acquired the basics of climbing technique
On the course we try to focus on more challenging routes working towards leading F6c and above, as well as red point and on-sight attempts.

All Rockbusters camps are dedicated to climbing but we also have a great time off the rock. Come with us and you get the whole climbing experience, both during the day and at night, when we enjoy kicking back and relaxing. We love to welcome new guests and try to make everyone feel like part of the family.

rows.title: Rockbusters Climbing EXPRESS
rows.shortDescription: Organising a climbing holiday can be a tricky business. Believe us, we know better than most. But we’ve also got bags of experience doing it so why don’t you sit back and let us handle the boring stuff for you? Enjoy climbing in some of Spain’s best destinations without all the hassle of renting cars, climbing gear and camping equipment. Simply tell us where you want to go and when, and we’ll do the rest. We’ve got all the contacts and local knowledge so we can sort everything, leaving you to count the days until you come join us.

catalogueCard.title: Rockbusters Climbing Express
catalogueCard.description: Tell Rockbusters where and when you want to climb, then let the team handle Spain trip logistics.

children.text: We will pick you up and drop you off at a previously arranged place (see the locations below) and take you climbing for as long as you like. It’s a unique chance, especially for experienced climbers looking for good quality routes and motivated company. Just choose your dates, book your flight and let us do the rest.

Rockbusters Climbing Express is for groups of a minimum of four people. You’ll be accompanied by one instructor/guide who’ll show you around the crags and will handle all the logistics. You can also pay a little extra for personalised climbing tuition to improve your climbing:
What equipment you need and how to choose it properly so that you have the best climbing experience and stay safe
How to belay, set up top-rope and lead climbing to develop more technical climbing skills
Using a guide book, climbing calls and communication so that you can tackle new climbing areas in the future
Basic movement skills for more efficient climbing
Basic understanding of outdoor risks so you can make it home safely every day
Cleaning the anchors so you can retrieve all your gear safely
Locations in Spain include: Rodellar, Siurana, Margalef, Terradets, Mongrony, Chulilla, Sella, Cuenca, Albarracin, Cacin, El Chorro.
We’re looking to expand the Rockbusters Climbing Express options into Germany, France, Italy and Czech so watch this space.

We work hard to make sure you have the best climbing experience possible, whenever and wherever you choose. With personal tuition you should improve quickly, achieving new climbing heights. But we also play hard and enjoy welcoming new guests. We aim to provide the ultimate climbing experience both on and off the rock face. So, expect the unexpected and come be part of the Rockbusters family.

rows.title: Spanish Climbing Trip
rows.shortDescription: The Rockbusters Spanish road trip is always one of our most popular events each year. It’s a tour that gives you a unique chance to discover the best Spanish crags. These are notoriously some of the best in the world so do yourself a favour and don't miss out. Trust us on this one. It’s an intense and epic tour that every climbing freak should experience.

catalogueCard.title: Spanish Climbing Trip
catalogueCard.description: Discover Spain's standout crags on an intense Rockbusters road trip through some of the world's best sport climbing areas.

children.text: Apart from getting a great introduction to great climbing areas all around Spain you’ll also benefit from some world-class guiding. Our top performance coaches will help you develop your skills and you’ll have a blast with some great climbing company. We guarantee you a varied month full of fun and loads of new climbing experiences. Try out a massive range of different styles too, from vertical fingery lines in Montserrat to overhanging boulders in Albarracin – plus plenty more.

Join the tour for as many weeks as you want. At the weekends we stop at nearby airports to drop off and pick up clients who can't make it for the whole trip. Although we’d love it if you could come from beginning to end and think you will too.
This is a Rockbusters climbing trip so expect to focus on the following:
Slab/vertical ground to improve footwork and climbing efficiency
Balance and foot placement to develop better technique for more confident climbing and strength building (leading comfortably F5 or more)
Overhangs and steep sections to develop strength and confidence on more challenging climbs (leading comfortably F6c or more)
On-sight/red point aimed at climbers who are confident enough with their balance, footwork and have already acquired the basics to progress at a faster rate

1st week: Sella/Costa Blanca

The biggest and best climbing area in the region, Sella boasts a load of easy and mid grade sport routes in the centre of the valley. Mid to harder grade routes are concentrated in steeper sectors like the famous ‘Wild Side’. There are also some bolted multi-pitch climbs in Pared de Rosaria, as well as entirely traditional routes in Puig Campana. All of this makes for some great quality limestone crags to crank.

Most of Sella’s routes are up to 30m of slabby or vertical, fingery and technical climbing on little crimps and holes. It can get a little busy but our expert guides know all the best spots to go to avoid the crowds. And, of course, this being Spain’s Costa Blanca, you can expect some pretty lovely climbing weather too.

2nd week: Albarracin (bouldering)

Albarracin is definitely the most important Spanish bouldering area, which is why we here there on our tour obviously. No other area in Spain compares to it. It’s even referred to as the Spanish Fontainebleau. The area is full of big, reddish sandstone blocks scattered around a beautiful forest. The stones are full of boulder problems of all difficulties and styles: roofs with big jugs, overhangs with crimps, as well as quality slabs.

There are fifteen different sectors, some of which have climbing restrictions from January to August but this doesn’t matter as there are always plenty of problems to solve. At 900m above sea level, the air is cool and dry enough to climb throughout the year. It’s also situated in a protected area, which means it remains a gorgeous place to climb.

3rd week: Margalef

At Margalef the crags are scattered around two little canyons, all very close to each other making for some convenient and intense climbing. The rock is a conglomerate, not too solid but great for climbing. It’s not like climbing at any other location here as you mostly climb over one, two or three finger pockets. Together with this are some slopers and crimps, and at some sectors tufas too.

You’ll find great lines of all difficulties from the 5th grade to the 9th, which is one reason why the area is so popular. Another is that once you get used to the style, red pointing is not as difficult as in more demanding areas such as nearby Siurana.

The grades in Margalef are a little softer but it doesn't take any qualities away from the place. It’s superb, good fun climbing in some stunning scenery where everybody finds what they’re looking for. From more remote, quiet and tranquil crags such as Catedral and Ermita or always busy and frantic crags just off the road, such as Raco de Finestra or Laboratori - it’s all here. An unusual but highly recommended stop off on our Spanish tour and one not to be missed.

4th week: Siurana

To some people, Siurana might look like little more than a mountain village perched on a cliff edge, living firmly in the past. To climbers, however, it looks more like paradise. Situated in the Tarragona mountains in the Sierra de Prades range, the yellow and grey limestone walls, slabs and overhangs are just begging to be explored. Come with our Rockbusters guides and that’s exactly what you’ll get to do all week.

The crags are situated between the tiny picturesque hamlet of Siurana and its larger neighbour, a village called Cornudella de Montsant. There are approximately 30 sectors and over 1,200 routes, most of them of superb quality. And new routes are still being opened up all the time. It’s also home to the legendary La Rambla route, first climbed by German Alexander Huber in 1994, and enough to test any climber in the world.
At less than an hour from other very important areas such as Margalef, Montsant, La Mussara and Arboli, the choice here is incredible.

We know that some or all of this sounds incredibly tempting. So be good to yourself and do the right thing – come and join our Spanish road trip. As one of our most popular tours, spaces get snapped up quickly so don’t hang around. You have been warned.

rows.title: Deep Water Solo / Mallorka
rows.shortDescription: At Rockbusters we love all areas and styles of climbing and we’re always first to try new things. We find the people who climb with us usually share the same kind of attitude. That’s exactly why we run our Deep Water Solo tours in Mallorca. Discover one of the best DWS and sport climbing destinations in Europe. Our team will show you around the area and will fill your days with some of the best and most challenging climbing you can imagine. Mallorca offers an incredible amount of epic routes in a relatively small area. It’s become famous for its world class DWS but in recent years loads of hot new crags have been bolted on the island. They’re definitely worth a visit too and makes for a really varied and exciting tour.

catalogueCard.title: Deep Water Solo Mallorca
catalogueCard.description: Explore Mallorca's deep-water solo cliffs and bolted sport crags with guides who know the island's best lines.

children.text: This trip is designed mainly for climbers who’ve already got some indoor climbing skills. Ideally you should know how to belay and tie on so that you can progress faster. This means it’s a great trip for anyone wanting to improve technique and get deeper into the climbing culture.

Spend some climbing time with our guides and their mates (soon to be your mates too). Get motivated climbing with the freaks and tackle as many tough routes as you can. If you like you, we can arrange some one-on-one coaching to get even more of your stay on the island.

As with all Rockbusters trips, we encourage a fun and friendly atmosphere which is more like climbing with good pals than instructors. We like to have fun on and off the face, so be ready to have some nighttime adventures too. It’s all about having a good time and living the climbing life.

Pushing yourself at DWS means you will be falling into the sea. Being confident swimming in open water is a requirement for this trip.
We welcome both novice and expert climbers. To get the most out of this trip we recommend that you be ready to push yourself to F5 (5.9). Grades range from F5 to F8 (5.9 - 5.13).
This is a climbing trip and our number one goal is to maximize your time spent on the rock.
The approaches range from 20-45 minutes and there are a couple of locations that will require scrambling over rock to access
To prepare for Deep Blue, you need gear for the salt and sea, as well as a backup kit for sport climbing in case the weather turns.
1. The Deep Blue Kit (DWS)
2+ Pairs of Climbing Shoes
: It takes some time to dry the rubber. Bring an older backup pair.
Liquid Chalk
: Use as a base layer so you don't need a chalk bag over the water.
20L–30L Dry Bag
: To keep your towel and snacks dry during boat approaches.
Snorkeling Goggles
: Vital for checking water depth and hazards before you jump.
2. Sport Climbing Backup (Rainy Days)
In case the conditions are not favorable for DWS, we head to sport crags. Bring your personal "redpoint" gear:
Harness & Helmet
: Ensure your harness has adjustable leg loops for comfort.
Chalk Bag
: For longer pitches where liquid chalk isn't enough.
Belay Device
: An assisted-braking device (like a Grigri) is best for long sessions.

Other recommended gear: a down jacket, a hat, a rain jacket, a pair of comfortable approach shoes, 2 bathing suits or quick-drying clothing, a towel, a headlamp, and a backpack big enough for carrying lunch and gear to the crag.

There is a basic shared accommodation organized by Rockbusters. We make sure everyone has a place to crash after hard day climbing. Our main goal is to integrate you into the local climbing communities and for these purposes, we use local climbing hostels, cottages, campsites, or places run by local climbers.
For accommodation of higher standards please make a personal inquiry through email/WhatsApp

rows.title: Cataluna Climbing
rows.shortDescription: On this trip to Catalonia you’ll get the chance to see and climb in some of the world's top sport climbing destinations. This includes Margalef, Siurana, Sierra de Monsant, Terradets, and Montserrat amongst others. This part of northern Spain is renowned for it’s awesome crags so why not let our ace instructors be your guide? Get to know areas famous for the hardest lines and popular among the strongest climbers in Europe. Taste the unique atmosphere of Spanish sport crags and get motivated with all the other cranking freaks on the rock.

catalogueCard.title: Catalunya Climbing
catalogueCard.description: Climb Catalonia classics including Margalef, Siurana, Montsant, Terradets, and Montserrat with Rockbusters guides.

children.text: We’ll belay you wherever you like and make sure you will be able to do as many climbs as your little fingers can manage during your stay. It’s all about maximising your time on the face. We will also provide you with one-on-one coaching, video and photo analysis to help improve your performance on the rock.
Our performance coaching is ongoing throughout the tour so here’s what you’ll learn:
What equipment you need and how to choose it properly so that you have the best climbing experience and stay safe
How to belay, set up top-rope and lead climbing to develop more technical climbing skills
Using a guide book, climbing calls and communication so that you can tackle new climbing areas in the future
Basic movement skills for more efficient climbing
Basic understanding of outdoor risks so you can make it home safely every day
Cleaning the anchors so you can retrieve all your gear safely

As well as all this, we’ll focus on slab/vertical ground and footwork. We’ll teach you how to use your balance and how to place your feet to achieve the most efficient way to move up on the rock (leading comfortably F5 or more). You’ll develop skills to help you handle steep rocks, save energy and climb more confidently and efficiently (leading comfortably F6c or more), with some work on overhangs too.

For climbers who are confident enough with their balance, foot work and who have already acquired the basics of climbing technique, we will move on to on-sight/red point. This means we can focus on more challenging routes (leading F6c and above). The emphasis is on quality climbing and reaching your climbing potential.

As you might expect, the Catalonia Advanced Climbing Trip is more suited to climbers who have some experience either indoor or outdoor. Beginners will probably be better suited to our novice courses. What this does mean is that we’ll be able to progress quickly and take on some of the tougher, more spine-tingling routes that this Spanish region can offer.
Get yourself signed up now.

rows.title: Girls On Rock
rows.shortDescription: Here at Rockbusters we always try to be different but we know that some climbing schools and climbers can be a bit macho. It’s not about who can climb highest or the fastest, it’s about challenging yourself and getting better. But because we know it’s sometimes a bit much, we’ve set up our girls only climbing trip. Of course, it might not be anything to do with all the macho rubbish, you might just fancy a girls trip away from all those smelly boys. And who can blame you? (Sorry lads but you’re all men enough to take it, right?)

catalogueCard.title: Girls on Rock
catalogueCard.description: A women-only climbing trip focused on progression, confidence, community, and getting better without the macho noise.

children.text: Whatever your reasons, our girls camps take place in the best sport climbing areas in Spain such as Sella, Teverga, Albarracin, Siurana, Margalef and Rodellar. There are unique opportunities for you to come and climb with girls who go hard and, more importantly, love every minute they spend on the rock.

Just pick the destination you prefer, book your flight, grab your harness and climbing shoes and come join us in sunny Spain. We guarantee new climbing experiences, progress and definitely loads of fun on and off the rock. We always try and create a warm and friendly atmosphere in all our camps but we find our girl only camps are always a little bit extra special.

Everyone is more then welcome, no matter which grades you climb. What matters to us is you being motivated to learn and progress. As a general rule (although not always) women usually have less strength than the guys but in our camp we’ll show you that’s not the be all and end all when it comes to your performance on the rock. See how the strength can be often replaced by precise technique and good mind control.

Specific climbing techniques, building up more confidence, getting faster and more explosive are among the things we will focus on with the goal of improving your climbing performance and overall feeling on the rock.
What you’ll learn:
What equipment you need for climbing and how to choose it properly so you’re always safe on a climb
How to belay, set up top-rope, lead and other technical aspects to build your knowledge base
Using a guide book so you can better know a climbing area
Climbing calls and communication so you won’t sound like a rookie
Basic movement skills for improved efficiency and better climbing
Cleaning anchors and basic understanding of outdoor risks so everyone goes home safe

As well as all of the above, we’ll focus on slab/vertical ground and footwork. We’ll teach you how to use your balance and how to place your feet to achieve the most efficient way to move up on the rock (leading comfortably F5 or more). You’ll develop skills to help you handle steep rocks, save energy and climb more confidently and efficiently (leading comfortably F6c or more), with some work on overhangs too.
So come on girls, sign up for our camp in Spain and lets show those boys how we do it.
